subject: Biology
title: Pollination Partnerships
description: A fast breakdown of Pollination Partnerships for builders.

hook.text: About 75% of the world's flowering plants depend on animals to carry their pollen.

buildup.text: Bees are the most important pollinators, visiting thousands of flowers each day.

discovery.text: Some flowers evolved to match one specific pollinator. Darwin predicted a moth for a deep orchid.

twist.text: That moth was found decades later—with a 30-centimeter tongue that matched the orchid perfectly.

climax.text: Pollinator decline threatens food crops worldwide. One in three bites of food depends on them.

punchline.text: No pollinators, no food. It's that simple.

quiz.question: What fraction of your food depends on animal pollinators?

details.summary: Pollination partnerships between plants and animals have co-evolved for over 100 million years. Bees, butterflies, birds, bats, and even lizards transfer pollen between flowers, enabling sexual reproduction in about 87 percent of all flowering plant species worldwide.
details.whyItMatters: Pollination supports 75 percent of global food crops and 87 percent of wild flowering plants. Declining pollinator populations from pesticides, habitat loss, and disease threaten food security and natural ecosystems worldwide.
takeaways: Approximately 87 percent of flowering plants require animal pollination
Bees are the most important pollinators for agriculture globally
Pollinator decline threatens billions of dollars in crop production yearly

faq.question: Why are bees declining worldwide?
faq.answer: Bees face multiple pressures including pesticide exposure especially neonicotinoids, habitat loss reducing wildflower availability, parasites like Varroa mites, and diseases. These stressors often interact, weakening bees' immune systems and reducing colony survival.

faq.question: What would happen without pollinators?
faq.answer: We would lose most fruits, vegetables, nuts, chocolate, and coffee. Entire ecosystems dependent on flowering plants would collapse. Wind-pollinated staples like wheat and rice would survive, but nutrition diversity would plummet and wild habitats would degrade drastically.
